Just personal preference, because I run Linux on a bunch of laptops that are often not on my home network, but I've found that setting these mounts to "noauto" in fstab, then creating a little script that I can launch from the desktop to mount the shares works better. Reason being, if network shares time out during the boot process, it can stall the boot, which is really annoying when you just want to bring the system up off-site real quick to check on something that takes less time than it takes for the mount commands to time out.

Vulkan As The Next-Gen Graphics API Is Poised To Reshape Mobile Gaming

I'm bullish about Vulkan, but it is far from establishing dominance. It will certainly make things better for mobile development and that is where I expect it to gain the most traction. However, many open source advocates believe that it will displace DirectX as the API of choice for PC gaming. I believe that is a far tougher challenge.

Although this article hints at why OpenGL failed against DirectX, it didn't seem to mention the fact that being Open Source actually impeded it's ability to improve as rapidly as DirectX. It remains to be seen if Vulkan development will be nimble enough. Vulkan has distinct advantages over DirectX, but it is starting at the back of the pack (for PC gaming) and it's fate largely depends on how many devs get on board. In a perfect world superior open APIs should prevail, but in the real world with market forces brought to bear it gets more complicated. Microsoft is strongly pushing DirectX to developers and incentivizing them to use it. They can make a compelling case given their market position and the ease of porting to the XBox One. And MS has the resources to keep making DirectX better whilst Vulkan may or may not be able to keep pace.

Ultimately I do think Vulkan will be a worthy successor to OpenGL, but it stands to run into the same hurdles that held OpenGL back as well. One thing it has going for it, however, is that it is being fully embraced by Android/Google so it will have at least one market it can dominate from the get-go.
Mobile might be the Trojan Horse that leads to wider adoption, and eventually better PC support.
